title: Oasis Two: the crossing, drawn
summary: They chart the crossing minute by minute, set the chart against a guess they wrote down before they opened the log, and then write version two of their own protocol card and are told plainly what that page is about to become.
materials: the pace log from the crossing, exactly as you wrote it on the day
your protocol card, version one, written in week 7
the half crossing debrief from week 5, for comparison
graph paper, a ruler and four or five coloured pencils
a fresh index card for version two, and a pen you like writing with
the expedition report form from week 3, open in the field journal
a paper clip, for the two cards

steps.title: How the second oasis runs
steps.body:
Oasis Two is not a test and it is not a post-mortem. It is the shade where you sit down and look at what the desert actually did to your hours.

The hour has two halves. First you draw the crossing: every minute of the window, on graph paper, coloured by what you were doing. Then you write version two of your own card.

The design loop runs the hour, pointed at a new question today. Ask: where did the time actually go, and where did it feel like it went? Imagine what the chart is going to look like before you draw a single line, and say that guess out loud so it cannot quietly rearrange itself later. Plan the chart before the ruler comes out: what runs across the page, what the colours stand for, where the submissions get marked.

Two rules for the whole hour, and they are the two the expedition report has carried since week 3. Route and weather, never a score: what happened, what you chose, what you would pack differently. And the log outranks the memory every single time, including when the memory is yours and it is very sure of itself.

One small thing before the graph paper, and it takes half a minute. Turn back to the dawn column in the field journal and run a finger down it: a date and two numbers for every morning you caught, a blank for every morning you did not. Do nothing to it and tidy nothing in it. In week 9 that column stops being a habit and becomes the data you do statistics on, blanks and all.

The keyboard and the pen are both yours. A grown-up may hold the other end of the ruler if you ask, and that is the whole of their job today.

Hand the device to a grown-up when you reach the next step. It is addressed to them.

steps.title: For the family only
steps.body:
Family, this step is for you. Hand the device back after reading it.

They are about to show you a chart of one morning of their own work, minute by minute. One thing ruins that and two things make it worth doing.

The thing that ruins it is asking how many they got. Do not ask, do not hint, do not congratulate a number. This report is route and weather. If the count comes up at all, it comes up because they decided to say it.

Good questions, all of them about the route. Which minutes bought the most? Which stretch would you spend differently next time? What were you doing in that long block before any typing started, and was it worth what it cost? What made you leave that problem, and what made you come back? Where did the chart surprise you?

The other thing that helps: let the gap between their guess and their log be interesting rather than embarrassing. Everybody has that gap, and it is not a character flaw. If one of you is willing to guess how long your own last hour of work took and then actually check it, do that out loud. A child this age learning that grown-ups are also bad at this learns something true.

One more. If the morning went badly, you will hear about it in this hour. Do not fix it, do not reframe it and do not tell them it does not matter. Ask what they would pack differently, and write their answer down where they can see you writing it.

Five minutes on the typing site before the ruler comes out. Home row first, then the words your crossing tongue actually uses, ten times each and no looking down: def, return, for, while, in, range, len, int, input, print, open, split.

C++ rides light this week and the Error Bestiary needs nothing but its pages tidied. Today's fingers belong to Python, because Python is the language every crossing runs in.

figure.alt: The same stretch of time judged two ways. While it happens, the length runs on attention: a wait you stare at feels slow. Afterwards, the length is rebuilt from memory: a stretch packed with different events reads as long later even if it flew by at the time. The two answers can honestly disagree, which is why the written log, not the memory, is what the chart trusts.

steps.title: The clock in your head is not a clock
steps.body:
You are about to compare two numbers that ought to be the same and will not be: how long a problem took, and how long it felt.

That gap is not a flaw in you. People do not read time off an internal clock, because there is no clock in there to read. What researchers generally find is that a stretch of time gets judged twice, in two different ways, and the two ways disagree on purpose.

While it is happening, the length runs on attention. The more of your attention lands on the waiting itself, the longer the wait feels. That is why staring at a problem you cannot start crawls, why a stretch spent absorbed in typing can vanish, and why watching a clock is the fastest known way to make time feel slow.

Afterwards it flips. Looking back, the length you report gets rebuilt out of what you remember happening. A stretch packed with different events reads as long in memory even though it flew by at the time, and an hour where nothing changed reads as short in memory even though it dragged while you sat in it.

So the same forty minutes can honestly feel short while you are inside it and long the next day, and neither report is a lie. They are answers to two different questions, asked of two different systems.

Which is exactly why the log wins. The log was written while the clock was still running, one line at a time, and it does not care how anything felt. Today you write your guess down first, face down, before you open it. Then you open it. The size of the gap is the finding.

And this is the mirage again, wearing a different costume. It looked right. It felt right. Neither of those is being right, and the only cure is checking against something that was measured rather than remembered.

figure.alt: The Oasis Two table: the coloured pace chart on graph paper laid flat, the folded felt-time guess opened out beside it, a ruler and coloured pencils nearby, and the family gathered round to read the chart rather than to hear a score.

steps.title: Chart the crossing
steps.body:
Before you open the log, and this part only works if you do it first. On a scrap of paper write down, from memory, how many minutes you think each problem took, which one ate the most, and how long you spent before you typed a single line of code. Fold it and put it face down on the table. That is the guess, and it counts.

Now open the log and build the chart.

Rule one long line across the graph paper for the whole window, marked off in ten-minute blocks, from the minute you opened the problems to the minute you stopped. Colour each stretch by which problem you were on, and keep a fourth colour for the minutes that belonged to no single problem: reading all the stories at the start, breaks, the walk, the staring.

Under that line rule a second strip, same scale, for what kind of work each stretch was: reading, drawing the farm on paper, typing, testing on the sample, submitting, waiting, parked.

Mark every submission on the top line with a tick where it happened, so you can see how the ticks are spaced.

Then three numbers in the margin, and these are the ones that will matter in September. Minutes on each problem. Minutes between opening the contest and typing your first line of code. Minutes after the last submission.

Now unfold the guess and lay it beside the chart. Do not tidy either one, and do not explain the guess away. For each place they disagree, write one short sentence naming which way the error went: did that stretch feel longer than it was, or shorter?

Then the question you ask the room out loud, which is the real point of the whole chart. Which minutes bought the most, and which minutes bought nothing at all? The answer is almost never the one people expect, and it is the first honest piece of the plan you are going to need in the fall.
checklist: I wrote my felt-time guess down and put it face down before I opened the log
The chart covers every minute of the window, coloured by problem, with a colour for the minutes that belonged to no problem
Every submission is ticked on the chart at the minute it happened
I worked out the minutes before my first line of code and the minutes after my last submission
I laid the guess beside the chart and wrote which way the gap went for each place they disagree

steps.title: The card, version two
steps.body:
Take version one out and read it aloud, line by line. Against each line put one of three marks: it held, it did not hold, or it was never needed.

A line marked did not hold is the most valuable line on the card, so do not hurry past it. There are only two ways a line fails. Either you did not follow it, in which case the new card has to say what would have made you follow it. Or you followed it and it made things worse, in which case it was wrong advice and it goes.

Now write version two on a fresh card, in your handwriting. The rule from week 7 has not changed: the contents are yours. Nobody dictates a line and nobody vetoes one, including the grown-up standing behind you who thinks they know a good one.

Three things are worth having on any version of this card, and the wording is still yours. What you do in the first ten minutes, before the editor is even open. How you decide a problem is parked rather than lost, and what has to be true before you come back to it. What you do in the two minutes after a submission comes back rejected, because those two minutes decide the next thirty.

One line belongs on the card that is not about you at all. Check the problem page for how it wants its input and output, every single time, and never carry an assumption over from last week's problem. The archive is not all one shape. Older contests name a pair of files and your program has to read and write those exact names; more recent ones use plain standard input and output. The page says which, and the page is the authority, not your memory of the last one you did.

Then the thing you get told plainly, because you should hear it now rather than work it out in September. This card is the first draft of your Autumn Protocol. When this season ends there is no weekly quest telling you what today is, and the fall runs on a page you wrote yourself. Version two is where that page starts.

Do not throw version one away. Clip them together. The pair is worth more than the newer one on its own, because the difference between them is the only record of what one dawn actually taught you.
checklist: I marked every line of version one as held, did not hold, or never needed
Version two is on a fresh card in my handwriting, and every line on it is mine
It says what I do before the editor opens, when a problem gets parked, and what I do after a rejection
It carries the line about checking the problem page for how it wants input and output
Version one is clipped to version two and nothing was thrown away

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt:
Photograph three things: the chart, the folded guess opened out beside it, and the two cards clipped together. If the chart is wider than the frame, photograph it in two overlapping halves.

Then add two lines of text. One: the biggest gap between felt and measured, named with the problem and the number of minutes. Two: the line on version two that was not on version one, and what put it there.

extras.title: Rewrite your best log
extras.body:
Your logs are the writing you do here, and writing gets better by rewriting, not by more of it. Pick your best log from this sprint and rewrite it once.

1. Read the log out loud. Mark every sentence that tries to say two things.
2. Rewrite so each sentence carries one idea. Split, do not shorten.
3. Find every adjective (hard, cool, weird) and replace it with a number or a fact: how many tries, how long, what broke.
4. Put the reason before the claim: "the loop ran twice, so the heart flashed twice" rather than "the heart flashed twice, because the loop ran twice".
5. Read both versions to someone and ask which one they could follow without you in the room.

What to notice: the rewrite is usually shorter and says more. That is the whole trick.
